Every quoted passage appears verbatim, and every date matches the document: IMF CR 16/381 is dated December 2016, the IMF 2025 Article IV is dated September 2025, OECD 2024 is dated March 2024, and the OECD 2026 survey and its executive summary are dated September 2026. All domains are tier 1.

Tension: the draft said the OECD reports total output growing 'well above trend' in the decade to 2024. The page says the opposite: recent growth 'has remained below trend, falling short of' the 1.8% average of that decade. I rewrote the tension so it only says that steady output growth (quoted) contrasts with 0.9 percent income-per-person growth. I also softened the population claim to 'which the sources tie to immigration'.

Arc: cut from 8 sentences to 6 to meet the 4–6 rule. I replaced 'strong institutions', which no opened source says, with the OECD's 'skilled workforce, good infrastructure'. I fixed the comparison that applied the 2016–2025 structural-peer median of 1.6 to both decades, and softened 'much of the growth in total output came from' immigration to 'lifted by', in line with the IMF's 'boosted by'.
Franc thread: 'hit exporters' became 'dented activity', matching the cited IMF passage.
Workers thread: dropped 'rather than from more output per person', which no cited passage supports.

Productivity thread: dropped 'Output per worker is among the highest in the world', which no cited passage supports (the OECD says 'among the highest in the OECD'). I re-cut the OECD quote to include the named sectors (pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, precision manufacturing, financial services) and extended the IMF quote to cover the lag in small firms and services. Both stay under 25 words.

Tariffs thread: changed 'Chemicals and pharmaceuticals lead Swiss exports', which is not in the cited passages, to 'Growth leans on chemicals and pharmaceuticals'. Changed 'move the whole economy' to 'weigh on'.

Since last year: dropped 'Pharmaceutical exports swung with these changes', which no opened page supports. In its place I added the OECD statement that export growth slowed sharply in late 2025, with a citation. Named the February 2026 ruling as the US Supreme Court's and added an OECD citation for it.

growth_story.headline: Switzerland's income per person has crept up 0.8 percent a year since 1990, carried by a few export stars and knocked by franc and tariff shocks.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990, income per person in Switzerland has grown slowly, averaging 0.8 percent a year over 1990–2025 with no lasting change in pace. The period started badly: income per person fell every year from 1990 to 1993 and did not get back to its 1990 level until 1997. After that, shocks kept growth low, each one followed by a recovery: the global crisis in 2009 (-3.2 percent), the jump in the franc after the floor against the euro was removed in 2015, and the pandemic in 2020 (-3.0 percent). Growth averaged 0.9 percent a year in 2006–2015 and again in 2016–2025, when the median among its structural peers was 1.6. The sources credit a skilled workforce, good infrastructure and a few very productive export industries led by pharmaceuticals, and they show total output lifted by a workforce enlarged by immigration. Income per person reached a new high in 2022 and has stayed just below it since, as US tariffs and a franc pushed up by safe-haven inflows put pressure on exports.

threads.title: The franc floor and its exit
threads.text: In global scares, money flowed into Switzerland as a safe haven and pushed the franc up, so the authorities set a floor against the euro and later removed it. When the floor ended in early 2015, the jump in the franc dented activity, and income per person grew only 0.3 percent that year.

threads.text: Total output has been lifted by a fast-growing workforce, many of them workers from abroad. That raises total output faster than income per person.

since_last_year.text: In August 2025 the United States sharply raised tariffs on most Swiss goods, and export growth slowed sharply in late 2025. A joint statement in November 2025 cut the tariffs, and a US Supreme Court ruling in February 2026 lowered them again. Income per person grew 0.3 percent in 2025 and remains just below its 2022 peak.

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Switzerland 2026

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Switzerland 2026
citations.quote: subsequently lowered further to 10% additional tariffs following the US Supreme Court ruling in February 2026

citations.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Switzerland 2026
citations.quote: Export growth decelerated sharply in late 2025 following the introduction of a 39% additional tariff on most merchandise imports by the US

growth_story.tension: The sources describe steady growth in total output: the OECD refers to "the annual average growth rate of 1.8% that the country has enjoyed in the decade leading up to 2024". Yet income per person rose only 0.9 percent a year over 2016–2025 and has stayed just below its 2022 peak. Most of the gap is population growth, which the sources tie to immigration.
